answer.evidence: The north and south walls each have a wall-walk top of about 32 rows: a crenellated parapet at the top (rows 48-58 on the north wall) and a flagstone walkway below it (rows 60-78). A dark front-edge line at row 79 (#4e3d30) closes the walk. Below that line is a 4-tile (about 64-row) ashlar front face, shown by the column scan at x=208 and x=303. Towers and gatehouses have crenellated top platforms that end in an edge line, then the front faces with arrow slits and arches. The west and east walls are shown from above as walkways. No receding isometric side face is drawn; the structure is a south-facing 3/4 view with visible tops.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 11 visible tones per tile, against 12 and 10 for the references, so density matches. Its ashlar is cut block by block with light tops, mid faces and dark joints, and the wall-walk tops use warmer orange-tan stones. Shadows form a separate dark brown step, giving about 5 steps on the sandstone ramp, close to the references' 5-6. Dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, and by eye the outlines are dark brown-tan versions of the stone rather than a black line. Forms are mostly separated by value, as in Beodeul. Near-flat coverage is 12%, mostly the sand road and a few plain wall patches, so it is slightly above the references' 0% but not a flat-fill problem. The wall ring is a large composite rather than a house. The main shortfall is that some wall faces are a little uniform and repetitive, with sparse speckle compared with the references' grain, but a careful artist would accept it next to them.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has about 11 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, so density is comparable. Its dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, which matches the picture: the outlines and block joints are dark brown-tan, tinted to the sandstone, with no black sticker line. A dark front-edge line at row 79 and a light lip at rows 80-81 follow, and the ashlar front face runs from about row 82 to 143 (roughly 64 rows). Towers and gatehouses repeat this pattern, each with a crenellated platform top, an edge line and a tall front face with slits, doors and arches. styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has about 11 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 in the references, so it is in the same range. Near-flat coverage is 12% against 0% for both references, so it has a few flat areas. They are the sandy road and the plain parapet and walkway bands. The 0% near-neutral share of dark edge pixels means the outlines carry a tint. By eye they are a dark brown-tan next to the sandstone, not black. The ashlar faces show about 5 steps: highlight, light, mid, shadow and deep joint, with per-block variation, speckle and shaded stones. The shadowed sides add more steps. The orange-brown wall-walk tops and the tower platforms show grain. The arch, doors with iron bands, torches, banners and slits add detail. The road is a flat fill with only sparse dots, and the references have no flat fills at all. Overall this is slightly thinner than the references in grain, but a careful artist could accept it next to them.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 11 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, so it is in the same range. Near-flat coverage is 12% against 0% for both references, so there are a few flat areas. Dark edge pixels are 0% near-neutral, so the outlines are tinted: dark brown-tan shading sits next to the sandstone, with no black sticker line. The ashlar faces have several stone tones (highlight, light, mid, shadow, deep joint) and per-block variation. The parapet crenellations and flagstones carry grain, and the terracotta-orange upper wall-walk has speckle. The shadow strips and dark tones at the wall bases add depth. The sand road and some wall-face blocks look a little uniform and repetitive compared with the references' per-tile grain. The reference roofs show richer per-tile highlights.
